passage:
Subject: Something I saw at work

Hi Vijay,

Remember how I used to say there are two kinds of people at work, the ones who follow orders and the ones who roll their eyes at every rule? This week I saw a third kind. Management announced that anyone taking leave in the audit quarter would lose their bonus, even for a family emergency. Most of us grumbled at lunch and said nothing upstairs. Kalpana did something else. She wrote to HR, copied our manager, and asked for it to go to the staff council. She didn't mock the policy, and she didn't skip work in protest. At the council she said, "I want this firm to do well. That's why I'm raising this." They agreed to exempt emergencies. I always thought loyalty meant keeping quiet. Apparently not.

Write soon,
Preeti

qa.q: What did management say would happen to anyone taking leave in the audit quarter?
qa.a: They would lose their bonus, even for a family emergency.

qa.q: How does Preeti feel about loyalty after watching Kalpana, and what shows it?
qa.a: Preeti seems surprised and impressed: she writes 'I always thought loyalty meant keeping quiet. Apparently not', so Kalpana's open objection now looks loyal too.

qa.q: Which choice made Kalpana's objection work where the lunchtime grumbling did not?
qa.a: She wrote to HR, copied the manager and asked for the staff council, so the concern reached people who could change the policy.

qa.q: How might the manager copied on Kalpana's email see her?
qa.a: The manager may see Kalpana as someone who cares about the firm, because she raised the issue openly and said she wanted it to do well.

grounding: A colleague watches a peer challenge an unfair leave policy through HR and the staff council, and sees that loyalty and principle can go together.

passage: Neelam leaned toward the microphone. "So, Swati, you want the story? I was two years into the night desk at the newspaper. The editor brought in a rule: no byline for anyone with under a year's service, even if they wrote the whole piece. Most juniors shrugged. One senior, Tomas, called it feudal and started leaving his own byline off in protest. Then there was Farzana. She'd written three front-page stories without her name. She didn't sulk, didn't sneer. She wrote a proposal for the editorial board: full bylines for staff, a 'with' credit for trainees. She presented it at the monthly meeting, calm, with dates and page numbers in hand. The board said yes. What stuck with me? She walked into that meeting wearing the paper's lanyard she was so proud of. I'd thought you had to choose, the paper or your principles. Farzana didn't."

qa.q: How many front-page stories had Farzana written without her name?
qa.a: Three front-page stories.

qa.q: What did Neelam come to believe after watching Farzana at the meeting?
qa.a: Neelam realised you don't have to choose between the paper and your principles, since Farzana was proud of the paper and still objected.

qa.q: What set Farzana's response apart from Tomas's, and why did it succeed?
qa.a: Tomas called the rule feudal and dropped his byline, while Farzana brought a calm proposal with dates and pages to the board, giving them something they could accept.

qa.q: How might the trainees be affected by the board's decision?
qa.a: They now get a 'with' credit instead of no name at all, so their work becomes visible because one person objected properly.

grounding: A colleague recalls a peer who challenged an unfair byline rule through a proposal to the board, without sneering, and learns loyalty and principle can coexist.

passage: My name's Yash. I sit two desks from Aadhya at the logistics firm, so I saw most of it. The new policy said drivers who reported a vehicle fault after hours would lose half a day's pay. Aadhya read the email, went still, and opened a blank document. I assumed she'd forward it round with a sarcastic line; I had one half-typed myself. She didn't. By evening she had a two-page note for the operations committee: how many faults were found after hours last year, what happens when drivers hide them, and an idea for a night reporting line. She sent it through the proper form and told our manager face to face that she had done so. I can't say what she felt. She looked calm, maybe tired. I deleted my half-typed forward that evening. A fortnight later the committee dropped the pay cut.

qa.q: What would drivers who reported a vehicle fault after hours lose under the new policy?
qa.a: Half a day's pay.

qa.q: What does Yash's deleted forward suggest about how Yash's thinking changed?
qa.a: Yash had planned to mock the policy, but watching Aadhya's careful note made sarcasm feel small beside a proper objection.

qa.q: What steps did Aadhya take that made her objection work?
qa.a: She wrote a two-page note with last year's figures and a night reporting idea, used the proper form, and told the manager face to face.

qa.q: How might the drivers see the committee's decision?
qa.a: The drivers no longer risk losing pay for reporting faults, so they can report them honestly instead of hiding them.

grounding: A colleague watches a peer object to an unfair pay policy through the proper committee without sarcasm or rule-breaking, and drops their own mockery.

passage:
Monday. The notice by the hotel kitchen's time clock said tips would now go only to waiters. Shankar, a line cook, expected Lokesh to explode; Lokesh had worked the tandoor for four years. Instead he read it twice, took a photo and went back to his skewers. He's scared, Shankar decided.
Thursday. At the staff council, Lokesh stood up with a typed page: the cooks' hours on banquet nights, and a request for a shared pool. When Venkat from the grill muttered that they should all slow down service to teach management a lesson, Lokesh shook his head. "I like this place. That's why I'm asking properly."
Three weeks later. The revised notice gave the kitchen a quarter share, less than Lokesh had asked for. Shankar watched him shake the manager's hand, and realised he had been wrong about which of them was scared.

qa.q: What share did the revised notice give the kitchen?
qa.a: The revised notice gave the kitchen a quarter share.

qa.q: What did Shankar first think Lokesh's quiet reaction meant, and why did that change?
qa.a: Shankar assumed Lokesh was scared, but the typed page and the calm refusal to slow down service showed that the quiet came from care for the place, not fear.

qa.q: When Venkat suggested slowing down service, what choice did Lokesh make, and why was it a turning point?
qa.a: He refused and stayed with the staff council, which kept trust with management and made a partial win possible.

qa.q: How might the hotel manager see Lokesh after the council, compared with a cook who slowed service in protest?
qa.a: The manager probably sees someone who cares about the hotel and can be reasoned with, which made the quarter share easier to agree to.

grounding: Over three weeks a cook watches a colleague challenge an unfair tip rule through the staff council without sabotage, and learns that loyalty and principle fit together.

passage:
"Ritu, you keep saying people who complain at work are troublemakers. Let your Nani tell you about Joseph.
I was twenty-four, a clerk in the mill office in Coimbatore. One monsoon the bus drivers struck for a week, and the management passed an order: anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay. Half of us walked six kilometres every morning.
Some clerks tore the notice down at night. Others paid and cursed. Joseph, who sat across from me, did neither. He kept coming on time, wrote to the works committee with the strike dates, and signed it in his own name. I was sure he'd be sacked.
He wasn't. The committee gave a half-hour grace on strike days. And Joseph still stayed late every Friday closing the accounts, same as before. That's when I understood a person can love a place and still tell it where it is wrong."

qa.q: What did the management order say about clocking in late?
qa.a: Anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay.

qa.q: What did Nani expect would happen to Joseph after the letter, and what does that suggest about her view back then?
qa.a: She was sure he'd be sacked and worried for him, which suggests she then saw objecting as risky and even disloyal.

qa.q: Which of Joseph's choices made the change possible, compared with the other clerks?
qa.a: He neither tore down the notice nor paid and cursed; he wrote to the works committee with dates and his own name, which the committee could act on.

qa.q: Why might Nani be telling Ritu this story now?
qa.a: Ritu calls people who complain at work troublemakers, and Nani wants Ritu to see that someone can object openly and still be loyal.

grounding: An elder recalls watching a colleague challenge an unfair late-pay order through the works committee while staying loyal, and what she learned from it.

passage:
It was quarter-end, the office was buzzing with deadlines, and Ganga had three reports due by six. Then the email came: all staff to work Saturdays for two months, unpaid.
People groaned. Some cursed the management in whispers. Someone said, "Just don't come. What'll they do?"
Gurleen, at the next desk, didn't whisper. She finished her work, then typed a formal note to HR and the manager, with the company's own leave policy attached. She asked for a meeting. In it she said, calmly, "I'm committed to this team. That's why I'm raising this properly."
Ganga watched her walk back to her desk, steady.
Ganga had always thought you either kept your head down or rebelled. She hadn't seen someone be loyal and principled at once.
Two days later, HR changed the Saturdays to paid overtime.

qa.q: How long were the unpaid Saturdays supposed to last?
qa.a: Two months.

qa.q: What was Ganga thinking as she watched Gurleen walk back?
qa.a: Ganga felt admiring and surprised, seeing that loyalty and principle could go together.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that others could learn from?
qa.a: She raised the objection formally with the company's own policy, asked for a meeting and stayed committed, using proper channels rather than sneering or skipping.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen Gurleen's approach?
qa.a: The manager might have respected her calm, committed way of raising it and found it harder to dismiss.

grounding: It shows a colleague seeing a peer object openly through proper channels and learning loyalty and principle can go together.

passage:
At the Kolkata newspaper office, Pradeep noticed the change first on the notice board: freelance photographers' names would no longer be printed with their photos.
In the canteen, reporters grumbled. "Typical." "Let's all stop crediting anyone." One joked about leaking it online.
Anirban didn't join in. At the Monday editorial meeting, he stood up with a folder. "I've worked here five years. I care about this paper," he said. "That's why I'm raising this. Freelancers depend on credits to get their next job. Here are three other papers' credit policies. I'd like us to reconsider."
The editor frowned but listened. "Put it in writing. We'll discuss it at the board."
Pradeep watched Anirban sit down, calm. He'd always thought objecting meant being against the paper. Anirban had just shown him it could mean caring for it.
Three weeks later, credits were back.

qa.q: How long had Anirban worked at the newspaper?
qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: What was Pradeep thinking as Anirban sat down?
qa.a: Pradeep felt admiring and a little surprised, realising objection could come from caring for the paper.

qa.q: What made Anirban's objection effective?
qa.a: He raised it in the proper meeting, explained who was harmed, brought other papers' policies and followed the editor's process.

qa.q: How might the freelance photographers see the change?
qa.a: They would probably feel relieved and respected, getting credit they need for future work.

grounding: It shows a colleague observing a peer object to an unfair policy through proper channels, loyal and principled at once.

passage:
"Jeevan, why did you do that in the meeting?" Disha asked as they walked out.
"Do what?"
"Object. To the mask policy. In front of the director."
"It's a bad policy. Cleaners shouldn't have to work in the chemical store without masks just to save money."
"But you could've just ignored it. Or complained in the chat group like everyone else."
"Complaining in the group changes nothing. And ignoring it means the cleaners still breathe that stuff."
"Weren't you scared?"
"A bit. But I followed the process. I sent it to the safety officer first. Then I raised it in the meeting."
"The director looked annoyed."
"Maybe. But I'm not against this company. I want it to be the kind of place that does this right."
Disha was quiet. "I didn't know you could do both."
"Both what?"
"Be loyal. And say no."

qa.q: Who did Jeevan send the objection to first?
qa.a: The safety officer.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when saying "I didn't know you could do both"?
qa.a: Disha felt surprised and admiring, realising loyalty and principled objection can go together.

qa.q: What steps did Jeevan follow, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Jeevan went to the safety officer first, then raised it in the meeting, using proper channels instead of grumbling or ignoring the rule.

qa.q: How might the cleaners be affected by Jeevan's objection?
qa.a: They could get masks and be protected from the chemicals, so they would likely feel relieved and cared for.

grounding: It shows a colleague seeing a peer object openly to an unfair policy through proper channels, and learning loyalty and principle fit.

passage:
I'm Tanuja, and I used to think that people who objected at work were either troublemakers or suck-ups. Then I watched Madhav.
Our call centre in Bengaluru brought in a policy: no toilet breaks outside the fixed two slots. Everyone grumbled in the canteen. Some people started faking system errors to get a break.
Madhav didn't grumble or fake anything. He wrote a calm email to HR with facts: pregnant colleagues, people on medication, a health guideline. He asked for a meeting. He still followed the slots while waiting.
Two weeks later, HR changed the rule. Madhav never bragged. He still stayed back to help the team lead.
I realised you can be loyal to your workplace and still stand for what's right.

qa.q: What did some people fake to get a break?
qa.a: Some people started faking system errors.

qa.q: How did Tanuja's feelings about objecting at work change after watching Madhav?
qa.a: Tanuja moved from seeing objectors as troublemakers to feeling admiration, realising loyalty and principle can go together.

qa.q: What made Madhav's objection work?
qa.a: He used calm facts, went through HR, asked for a meeting, and kept following the rule while waiting.

qa.q: How might the pregnant colleagues have been affected by the rule change?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and cared for, able to take breaks when they needed.

grounding: A colleague watches a peer object calmly to an unfair break policy through proper channels and learns loyalty and principle can go together.

passage:
Shift supervisor's note, warehouse, Nagpur

This month the company announced that anyone late by five minutes would lose a full day's pay. Several workers were angry and one talked of blocking the loading bay.
Kiran, the other shift supervisor, did something different. She collected data on bus delays from the new ring road, met the operations head, and proposed a fair grace period with warnings. She kept enforcing the current rule on her shift while waiting.
I was surprised. I'd assumed Kiran would either stay silent to please management or side with the protesters. Eshaan, a new loader, asked me why she bothered. I said, "Because she believes in the rules, and in fixing them."
The policy was changed to a warning system last week.

qa.q: What did Kiran propose to the operations head?
qa.a: She proposed a fair grace period with warnings.

qa.q: Why did the note-writer feel surprised by Kiran?
qa.a: The note-writer felt surprised and impressed that Kiran neither stayed silent nor joined the protest, but objected through proper channels.

qa.q: Why did Kiran's approach work better than blocking the loading bay?
qa.a: She used data and a meeting, kept enforcing the rule meanwhile, and got the policy changed fairly without disrupting work.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see Kiran after the note-writer's answer?
qa.a: Eshaan may start seeing her as someone who respects rules and also works to make them fair.

grounding: A supervisor watches a peer object to an unfair lateness policy through proper channels and sees loyalty and principle together.

passage:
Diary, Thursday

Saw something today I keep thinking about. Our bank branch got a new target: every customer must be pushed a credit card, even pensioners. Most of us just did it, grumbling. A couple of people started quietly skipping it and lying in the reports.
Tanuja didn't do either. She wrote to the regional manager with examples of elderly customers who were confused and upset, asked for an exemption for pensioners, and kept following the target for everyone else while she waited.
I, Saurabh, honestly thought she'd get in trouble. Instead the manager called her, thanked her, and the rule was changed yesterday.
She's still the first one in and the last one out. Loyal and principled. I didn't know you could be both.

qa.q: Who did Tanuja write to?
qa.a: She wrote to the regional manager.

qa.q: How does Saurabh feel after seeing Tanuja's objection succeed?
qa.a: Saurabh is surprised and admiring, having feared Tanuja would get in trouble.

qa.q: What made Tanuja's objection principled rather than rebellious?
qa.a: She gave real examples, asked for a specific exemption through the proper person, and kept following the rule while waiting.

qa.q: How might elderly customers be affected by the rule change?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and respected, no longer pushed toward products they found confusing.

grounding: A colleague watches a peer object openly through proper channels to an unfair sales target and learns loyalty and principle can go together.

passage: In the block office at Rampur Kasba, Asif shared a table with Bidisha, and for three weeks he watched old women with thumbprint-smudged papers being turned away. The new order said ration card changes were online only. Most of them had no phone. Asif grumbled about it at lunch, like everyone. Bidisha did something different. She kept following the order, sitting with each woman to fill the form on the office computer herself. And on Friday she put a signed note in the officer's tray, listing forty-three names and asking for a paper-form window two days a week. Asif expected her to be scolded. Instead the officer called a meeting. Walking home, Asif kept thinking: she never once said the rule was stupid. She just tried to make it better, from inside.

qa.q: How many names did Bidisha list in her note?
qa.a: Forty-three names.

qa.q: What did Asif expect when Bidisha put the note in the tray, and how did he feel?
qa.a: Asif expected her to be scolded and felt nervous for her, assuming that objecting would look disloyal.

qa.q: What could Asif do now instead of grumbling at lunch?
qa.a: He could help the women fill the online forms too, or add his own signed observations to Bidisha's note for the meeting.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see her own role in the office?
qa.a: Bidisha seems to see herself as loyal to the office and to the women at once: following the order while asking, with evidence, for it to change.

grounding: In a small-town office a colleague watches a peer follow an unfair order while formally asking for it to change.

passage: In the Lisbon call centre, Astrid had worked beside Rafael for two years, and she had always filed him under 'nice, quiet, follows everything'. So she nearly spilled her coffee when, at the Monday meeting, he stood up about the new policy docking pay for bathroom breaks over five minutes. He didn't shout. He said he had been timing the breaks, that the rule hit the two pregnant colleagues hardest, and that he had submitted a written objection to the works council that morning. 'Until they decide, I'll follow it,' he added, and sat down. Astrid watched the manager's face go from annoyed to thoughtful. At lunch she asked, 'Aren't you afraid they'll see you as a troublemaker?' Rafael shrugged. 'I like this job. That's why I want it fair.' Astrid went back to her desk and read the policy properly for the first time.

qa.q: Where did Rafael submit his written objection?
qa.a: To the works council that morning.

qa.q: What was Astrid feeling when Rafael stood up at the Monday meeting?
qa.a: Astrid was startled and surprised, having filed Rafael as a quiet rule-follower, to see him object calmly and publicly.

qa.q: What might Astrid do after reading the policy properly?
qa.a: She could decide whether she agrees with Rafael and, if so, add her own written view to the works council rather than just grumbling.

qa.q: How does Rafael connect liking the job with objecting?
qa.a: Rafael sees fairness as part of caring about the job, so objecting through the works council is loyalty, not trouble.

grounding: A colleague abroad watches a quiet peer object to an unfair policy through proper channels while still obeying it.

passage:
The staff meeting at the girls' school in Lucknow was nearly over when the principal read out the new rule: any student more than five minutes late would be sent home for the day.
Parveen, in her second year of teaching, watched Salma raise her hand. Salma had been at the school twelve years and never missed a single duty.
"Ma'am, I support punctuality," Salma said evenly. "But forty of our girls come on the village bus, and it runs late three days a week. I've listed the dates. I'd like to request, in writing, a separate gate register for bus students."
Nobody laughed. Nobody rolled their eyes. The principal took the paper and said the committee would review it on Friday.
Parveen felt something shift. She had thought you either obeyed rules or grumbled in the corridor. Salma had done neither.

qa.q: How many of the girls come on the village bus?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: What did Parveen feel as Salma spoke?
qa.a: Parveen felt surprised and admiring, seeing a way between obeying silently and grumbling in the corridor.

qa.q: Which parts of Salma's objection made it principled rather than rebellious?
qa.a: She said she supported punctuality, brought the dates as evidence, and made a written request through the committee instead of sneering at or ignoring the rule.

qa.q: How might Salma see her own role at the school?
qa.a: Salma likely sees herself as loyal to the school, never missing a duty, and speaking up because she cares about its students, not to oppose it.

grounding: A young teacher watches a senior colleague object to an unfair rule through proper channels and learns that loyalty and principle can go together.
